chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, all from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Malik ibn Ayn, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a Christian who died, leaving a son of his Muslim brother and a son of his Muslim sister, and the Christian had children and a Christian wife. children and a Christian wife. He (peace be upon him) said: 'I see that the son of his Muslim brother should be given two-thirds of what he left, and the son of his Muslim sister should be given one-third of what he left, if he does not have young children. But if he has young children, then upon the two inheritors is that they should spend upon the young children from what they inherited from their father, until they mature.'

It was said to him (peace be upon him): 'How should they spend?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The inheritor of the two-thirds should take out two-thirds of the expenses, and the inheritor of the one-third should take out one-third of the expenses. And if they mature, they cease the expenses for them.'

It was said to him (peace be upon him): 'And if the children become Muslim while they are young?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever their father left should be handed over to the Imam (peace be upon him) until they mature. If they remain upon Islam, the Imam hands over their inheritance to them. And if they do not remain upon Islam when they mature, the Imam hands over their inheritance to the son of his brother and the son of his sister, the two Muslims. He hands over to the son of the brother two-thirds of what was left, and he hands over to the son of the sister one-third of what was left.'
ai.seo_question: What are the inheritance rules for a Christian leaving Muslim cousins and non-Muslim minor children?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the specific inheritance distribution for a Christian decedent, prioritizing Muslim agnatic cousins (son of brother and son of sister) over non-Muslim offspring, reflecting the Shia principle of 'al-muslim yurath wa la al-kafir' (the Muslim inherits, but the non-Muslim does not). It further establishes a practical mechanism where the Muslim heirs bear the financial responsibility for the minors' maintenance, ensuring their upbringing is supported from the estate itself. The ruling also accounts for the theological status of the minors, stipulating that if they convert to Islam before maturity, their share is held in trust by the Imam until they reach adulthood, safeguarding their potential claim to the inheritance.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father and Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, and a number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad, altogether from Al Hassan Bin Mahboub, from Hisham Bin Salim, from Malik Bin Ayn, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘I asked him<sup>asws</sup> about a Christian who died and for him was a son of his Muslim brother, and a son of a Muslim sister, and for the Christian were children and a Christian wife.

So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘I<sup>asws</sup> see that you should give the son of his brother two-thirds of what is left (as legacy), and give the son of his sister a third of what is left, if there does not happen to be young children for him. So if there were small children for him, so it would be upon the two inheritors that they should spent upon the small children from what they both had inherited from their father, until they mature’.

It was said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘How should the two of them be spending?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The inheritor of the two thirds of the inheritance should take out two thirds of the expenses, and the inheritor of the one-third of the inheritance should take out a one-third of the expenses about them’.

It was said to him<sup>asws</sup>, so if the children become Muslim and they are still young?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Hand over to the Imam<sup>asws</sup> whatever their father had left until they grow up. So if they remain upon Al-Islam, the Imam<sup>asws</sup> hands over their inheritance to them, but if they do not remain upon Al-Islam when they mature, the Imam<sup>asws</sup> hands over their inheritance to the son of his brother, and the son of his sister, the two Muslim. To the son of the brother two-thirds would be handed over, and to the son of the sister, a one-third of whatever was left (as legacy)’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and a number of our people have narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad all from al-Hassan ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Malik ibn ’A‘yan, who has narrated the following: “I once asked abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a Christian man who has died.

The son of his brother is a Muslim and a son of his sister is a Muslim. The Christian man has children and a Christian wife. He (the Imam) said, ’Two-thirds of his legacy must be given to the son of his brother. One-third must be given to the son of his sister if he does not have any children who are small. However, if he has small children, then the heirs must pay for the maintenance of the small children from the legacy their father has left behind until they become mature.’
It then was asked from him (the Imam), ‘How must the two spend?’

He (the Imam) said, ‘The one who has received two- thirds must pay two-thirds of the maintenance and the one who has received one-third must pay one- third of maintenance until they become mature at which time they can discontinue payment for them.’ It then was asked, ‘What happens if the children become Muslims when they are small?’ He (the Imam) said, ‘Whatever their father has left behind must be given to the Imam until they become mature. If they remain Muslims the Imam gives their legacy to them. However, if they did not remain Muslims when they become mature, the Imam gives the legacy to the son of his brother and the son of his sister who are Muslims. Two-thirds of what is left is given to the son of his brother and one-third of what is left to the son of his sister.’”
